record.paper_title: Retrieving Convex Bodies from Restricted Covariogram Functions
record.context_brief: Strictly convex globally non-symmetric planar bodies
record.original_question: Let K and H be planar convex bodies. Let g_K be the covariogram of K, let D_K = {x - y : x and y are in K} be the difference body of K, let bd D_K be its boundary, and let o be the origin. For a closed set X, say GC(X) holds when g_K(x) = g_H(x) for all x in some neighborhood of X. Suppose K is strictly convex and has no local symmetry, where a local symmetry is a pair of closed boundary arcs of K that are reflections of each other in a point, have disjoint nonempty relative interiors, and are not properly contained in a larger pair with the same properties. If X is either {o} or bd D_K and GC(X) holds, must K and H coincide up to translations and point reflections, even when K is not assumed to have a twice continuously differentiable boundary with all principal curvatures nonzero?

evidence.quote: GC(X) The equality gK(x) = gH(x) holds for all x in some neighbourhood of X.

A pair of closed boundary arcs of a planar convex body K is said to be a local symmetry of K if they are reflections of each other in a point, have disjoint and nonempty relative interiors, and they are not properly contained in a pair of boundary arcs with the same properties. A planar convex body K is called locally symmetric if it possesses a local symmetry. Planar convex bodies without local symmetries are called globally non-symmetric.
It is known that the support of gK is the difference body of K, DK = {x − y : x, y ∈ K}, and that DK is o-symmetric.
II. If K is globally non-symmetric and X is either {o} or bd DK, then GC(X) implies the coincidence of K and H, up to translations and reflections.

It is an open question whether Part II of the above theorem holds for all strictly convex K not necessarily C 2 + . The positive answer to this question would imply the confirmation of Matheron’s conjecture for all planar convex bodies.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $K, H \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be planar convex bodies. The covariogram of $K$ is the function $g_K : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $g_K(x) = \mathrm{area}(K \cap (K+x))$. The difference body of $K$ is $D_K = \{x - y : x, y \in K\}$, and $\mathrm{bd}\, D_K$ denotes its topological boundary. Let $o$ denote the origin. For a closed set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, say that condition $\mathrm{GC}(X)$ holds if $g_K(x) = g_H(x)$ for all $x$ in some open neighbourhood of $X$.

A local symmetry of a planar convex body $K$ is a pair $(\alpha, \beta)$ of closed boundary arcs of $K$ such that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are reflections of each other in some point, have disjoint and nonempty relative interiors, and are not properly contained in any larger pair of arcs with these same properties. The body $K$ is said to be globally non-symmetric if it admits no local symmetry.

Assume that $K$ is strictly convex and globally non-symmetric, and assume $\mathrm{GC}(X)$ holds where $X$ is either $\{o\}$ or $\mathrm{bd}\, D_K$. Without imposing any further regularity on $\partial K$ (in particular, without assuming that $\partial K$ is of class $C^2$ with everywhere nonzero principal curvature), must $K$ and $H$ coincide up to translations and point reflections?
artifact.status_search_result: The covariogram problem in the plane was settled affirmatively by Averkov and Bianchi (2009), who proved Matheron's conjecture for all planar convex bodies, removing earlier C^2-type regularity hypotheses. Consequently the local-versus-global determination results (including the variant asked here for strictly convex globally non-symmetric planar bodies without C^2 boundary) follow from this more general resolution. The status is therefore solved.

status_evidence.title: Retrieving convex bodies from restricted covariogram functions
status_evidence.snippet: Paper deals with local determination of planar convex bodies from covariogram on neighborhoods of {o} and bd D_K.
status_evidence.claim: This is the source-context arXiv preprint addressing the local covariogram problem in the plane.

status_evidence.title: The Covariogram Problem (survey, Bianchi)
status_evidence.snippet: Most convex bodies in R^m are uniquely determined (up to translation and reflection) by their covariogram; in the plane Matheron's conjecture is confirmed for all planar convex bodies.
status_evidence.claim: The planar covariogram problem is fully solved, without C^2 regularity assumptions.
